citation-1.title: Geographically Weighted Regression: A Method for Exploring Spatial Nonstationarity
citation-1.abstract: Geographically weighted regression (GWR) is a method for exploring spatial nonstationarity. This paper describes the technique and its application, particularly with regard to the fit of spatial models.
reference_mentions: Various spatial prediction models [21] and spatial data analysis tools [24] have been developed to support geographic analysis. In this work, we focus on two local spatial models widely used in spatial analysis: Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR) [1], and its recent extension, Multiscale Geographically Weighted Regression (MGWR) [2]. GWR extends the classical linear regression model [20] by capturing spatial heterogeneity with influence spreading over the space in a constant scale. MGWR further improves GWR models where local influences are modeled in different spatial windows.

- [1] C. Brunsdon, A. S. Fotheringham, and M. E. Charlton. Geographically weighted regression: A method for exploring spatial nonstationarity. _Geographical Analysis_, 28(4):281–298, 1996. doi: 10.1111/j. 1538-4632.1996.tb00936.x 1

citation-2.title: Multiscale Geographically Weighted Regression (MGWR)
citation-2.abstract: Multiscale geographically weighted regression (MGWR) is developed to simultaneously estimate parameters at multiple scales and to produce a local statistic of goodness-of-fit for model evaluation. MGWR is based on the conventional geographically weighted regression (GWR), but allows the bandwidth to vary across space for different predictor variables, leading to a more flexible modeling framework. Empirical results from a case study on house prices in the Greater Toronto Area demonstrate that MGWR improves the explanatory power of GWR and provides richer insights into spatial heterogeneity. MGWR is shown to be a versatile tool for analyzing spatially varying relationships in diverse disciplines.

citation-3.title: NewsViews: an automated pipeline for creating custom geovisualizations for news
citation-3.abstract: NewsViews is a system that creates custom geovisualizations for news articles automatically, enabling readers to visualize the geographical context of stories. We describe its design and implementation, as well as a user study that demonstrates its utility.
reference_mentions: The design space of narrative visualization [18, 5] has been widely explored in the visualization community and a diverse set of storytelling and annotation methods have been developed to reveal observations in data and to convey key messages to an audience. Such narrative visualization techniques have been adopted by a variety of geovisual analytics applications [16] that have integrated story authoring tools with spatial data visualizations. For example, NewsViews [3] generates interactive maps with narrative annotations automatically from a given news article. Latif and Beck [10] introduce a bivariate map design that integrates template-based text annotations, and they later extend their work to investigate the interplay of text and visualization in geographic storytelling [11].

- [3] T. Gao, J. Hullman, E. Adar, B. Hecht, and N. Diakopoulos. NewsViews: An automated pipeline for creating custom geovisualizations for news. _Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems_, pp. 3005–3014, 2014. doi: 10.1145/ 2556288.2557228 1

citation-4.title: Visualizing Multiple Variables Across Scale and Geography
citation-4.abstract: Visualizing high-dimensional data is a challenging task in computer graphics, particularly when representing multiple variables that span different scales and geographies. In this paper, we present a comprehensive framework that enables users to visualize and interact with varying datasets, incorporating techniques such as dimensionality reduction and geographic mapping. We evaluate our approach through a series of use cases and highlight the significance of effective visualization strategies in understanding complex data structures.
reference_mentions: Most closely related to our work are the techniques that explain models from feature-level observation. Muhlbacher and ¨ Piringer [14] facilitated feature selection and optimization in regression models by partitioning the feature space into disjoint regions for visualization. Sedlmair et al. [17] proposed an abstract conceptual framework to discuss the visual parameter space analysis problems independent of the application domain. Goodwin et al. [4] extended visual parameter space analysis to the spatial domain, enabling the exploration of correlations between multiple variables that vary geographically at different spatial scales. While these techniques focus on explanations for domain experts, our work is designed to support explanations to experts and support their use of external information to contextualize these relationships and communicate their findings to a general audience. Our choice of text templates, as opposed to large language models, for narrative generation is to support control for reliability and reproducibility. All text generated must have a verifiable source and the generation of text for the analysis should always return the same results to ensure that the resulting analyses are not subject to misinformation.

- [4] S. Goodwin, J. Dykes, A. Slingsby, and C. Turkay. Visualizing multiple variables across scale and geography. _IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics_, 22:599–608, 1 2016. doi: 10. 1109/TVCG.2015.2467199 2

citation-5.title: Visualization Rhetoric: Framing Effects in Narrative Visualization
citation-5.abstract: The effective use of visualization depends not only on its technical attributes but also on how it is framed and perceived. We study visualization rhetoric as a critical factor impacting user interpretation of visualizations. Our focus is on narrative visualizations, which frame data-driven stories for audiences. We report on a user study that investigates how different framing strategies can lead to varied interpretations of the same underlying data.
reference_mentions: The design space of narrative visualization [18, 5] has been widely explored in the visualization community and a diverse set of storytelling and annotation methods have been developed to reveal observations in data and to convey key messages to an audience. Such narrative visualization techniques have been adopted by a variety of geovisual analytics applications [16] that have integrated story authoring tools with spatial data visualizations. For example, NewsViews [3] generates interactive maps with narrative annotations automatically from a given news article. Latif and Beck [10] introduce a bivariate map design that integrates template-based text annotations, and they later extend their work to investigate the interplay of text and visualization in geographic storytelling [11].

- [5] J. Hullman and N. Diakopoulos. Visualization rhetoric: Framing effects in narrative visualization. _IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics_, 17(12):2231–2240, 2011. doi: 10.1109/ TVCG.2011.255 1
